preamble: Unrounding of the close central rounded vowel [ʉ] to [ɨ]. Early (Old) Welsh had a rounded /ʉ(ː)/ beside unrounded /ɨ/; the rounded vowel arose from the monophthongization of several diphthongs and in Latin loans with ō or ū (Llun 'Monday' < Latin (dies) Lūnae, ffurf 'form' < Latin fōrma). Willis (2009) describes the distinction between /ɨ/ and /ʉ/ as lost in all contexts during Middle Welsh, the two merging as [ɨ]. Rounding survived longer in stressed than in unstressed syllables, and confusion of the spellings <u> and <y> appears from the fourteenth century onwards (gyrry 'drive' with <y> for historical /ʉ/). In monosyllables before /x/ the rounding was kept as an off-glide: Middle Welsh spellings such as ywch /ɨwx/ 'higher' (earlier uch) show the merger, and the off-glide gives modern uwch 'higher' and buwch 'cow' beside uchel 'high' and buchod 'cows'. Welsh spelling still writes historical /ʉ/ as u. Northern Welsh pronunciations have [ɨ] in these words; Southern Welsh ones have [i] (llu /ɬiː/), which is not part of this change.

examples.note: From Proto-Celtic *koilos; Willis (2009) lists cul among the Late Brythonic /ʉː/ words. In South Wales it is /kiːl/, a homophone of cil 'corner'.

sources: Willis, D. (2009). Old and Middle Welsh. https://davidwillis.net/old_and_middle_welsh.pdf
